procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Magistrate issuing summons to the appellant and others for charges under ss. 149, 341, 342, 352, 500 and 504 of the Indian Penal Code read with s. 34 thereof.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Sessions Judge recommended that the Magistrate be directed to require the complainant to obtain the requisite sanction before prosecuting the appellant. This matter was heard by a bench consisting of the Judicial Commissioner and the Additional Judicial Commissioner. The Judicial Commissioner was of the view that there was no material on the record to come to the conclusion that the acts complained of would be protected by the provisions of s. 197 (1) of the Code. The learned Additional Judicial Commissioner took a contrary view and held that sanction was necessary. The order of the court was that there being no third Judge to resolve the difference of opinion, the order of the learned magistrate issuing the summons be confirmed in terms of proviso to s. 7 (2) of the Goa, Daman and Diu (Judicial Commissioner's Court) Regulation, 1963.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave challenging the judgment and order dated November 19, 1966, of the Judicial Commissioner Court, Goa, Daman and Diu in Criminal Reference No. 103 of 1966. The sole point for decision in this appeal by special leave is whether a complaint which had been filed against the appellant and four other persons by the respondent for various alleged offences could be entertained without necessary sanction being obtained for the prosecution of the appellant, who at the material time, was the Deputy Superintendent of Police, under s. 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

directions: It would be open to the appellant to establish during the course of further proceedings that the requisite sanction under s. 197 must be obtained.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution against the appellant, a public servant, is invalid at the initial stage for want of sanction under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, on the basis that the acts alleged in the complaint were committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of official duty.

facts: The appellant, a Deputy Superintendent of Police, was accused in a private complaint of intervening in a land dispute between the complainant and some hawkers.
The complainant alleged that the appellant came to the spot, threatened and assaulted him, and then directed the hawkers to enter upon and take possession of the disputed land.
law: The Court referred to Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), which requires prior sanction to prosecute a public servant for an offence alleged to have been committed 'while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty.'

The Court reiterated the established legal principle that not every offence committed by a public servant requires sanction. There must be a 'reasonable connection' between the act and the official duty.
The act must be directly concerned with the official duties, allowing the accused to claim, reasonably and not fancifully, that it was done in the performance of their duty.
The decision on whether sanction is required at the initial stage is based on the allegations made in the complaint.
application: The Court analyzed the allegations in the complaint to determine if the appellant's actions were connected to his official duties.
It found that the alleged acts—taking sides in a civil dispute, threatening a citizen, and forcing one party to give up possession of land to another—were not part of a police officer's duty.
The Court noted that while a police officer can intervene to prevent a breach of peace, the complaint did not suggest such a situation existed.
Therefore, the Court could not find a reasonable connection between the alleged acts and the appellant's official duties as a police officer.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that based on the allegations in the complaint, the acts were not committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of official duty. Consequently, no prior sanction under Section 197 Cr.P.C. was necessary for the court to take cognizance of the complaint at that initial stage.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution against the appellant, a public servant, is invalid at the initial stage for want of sanction under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, on the basis that the acts alleged in the complaint were committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of official duty.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution is invalid because the previous sanction required under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to prosecute a public servant was not obtained.

The acts alleged in the complaint were committed while the appellant was acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty, thus necessitating prior sanction for the court to take cognizance of the offence.
respondent_arguments: The acts complained of (trespass, wrongful restraint, assault, and threats) were not committed in the discharge of the appellant's official duty.

Based on the allegations in the complaint and the complainant's initial statement, it was not established that the appellant was acting in his official capacity as a police officer when the alleged incident occurred.
Since the complaint does not show a connection between the alleged acts and the appellant's official duty, no sanction under Section 197 is required for the court to proceed.

cases.case_name: Ronald Wood Matham v. State of West Bengal
cases.principle: The question of whether sanction under s. 197 was necessary for charges of conspiracy and bribery was concluded by prior Judicial Committee decisions and must be answered in the negative.

cases.case_name: H. H. B. Gill v. The King
cases.principle: Sanction under s. 197 is not necessary for instituting proceedings on charges of conspiracy and bribery.

cases.case_name: Phanindra Chandra Neogy v. The King
cases.principle: Sanction under s. 197 is not necessary for instituting proceedings on charges of conspiracy and bribery.

cases.case_name: Matajog Dubey v. H. C. Bhari
cases.principle: There must be a reasonable connection between the act and the discharge of official duty; the act must bear such relation to the duty that the accused could lay a reasonable, but not a pretended or fanciful claim, that he did it in the course of the performance of his duty.

cases.case_name: Amrik Singh v. State of Pepsu
cases.principle: Sanction under s. 197(1) is not required for every offence committed by a public servant, but is necessary if the act complained of is directly concerned with his official duties so that, if questioned, it could be claimed to have been done by virtue of the office.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: There must be a reasonable connection between the act and the discharge of official duty; the act must bear such relation to the duty that the accused could lay a reasonable, but not a pretended or fanciful claim, that he did it in the course of the performance of his duty.
obiter: The jurisdiction of the court to proceed with the complaint emanates from the allegations made in the complaint and not from what is alleged by the accused or what is finally established in the case as a result of the evidence recorded.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Based on the allegations in the complaint, the appellant's actions were not part of his official duties. It is no part of the duty of a police officer to take sides in a property dispute and decide the dispute in favour of one party or the other, or to force one party to give up possession to the other, even if he was satisfied that the party seeking to take possession was lawfully entitled to do so. A police officer could only do this if there had been a direction by a competent court for rendering help in the matter of delivery of possession.
legal_tests_applied: There must be a reasonable connection between the act and the discharge of official duty; the act must bear such relation to the duty that the accused could lay a reasonable, but not a pretended or fanciful claim, that he did it in the course of the performance of his duty.

It is not every offence committed by a public servant which required sanction for prosecution under s. 197 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure nor even every act done by him while he was actually engaged in the performance of his official duties.

If the act complained of was directly concerned with his official duties so that, if questioned, it could be claimed to have been done by virtue of the office, then sanction would be necessary and that would be so, irrespective of whether it was in fact, a proper discharge of his duties or not.
why_appellant_lost: The court found that the acts alleged in the complaint—namely, taking sides in a private property dispute and forcing one party to give up possession without a court order—do not constitute the official duty of a police officer.

The appellant could not establish a reasonable connection between the alleged acts of trespass, assault, and threats and the discharge of his official duty as a police officer, as required by the legal test for sanction under Section 197.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the respondent's argument that the allegations in the complaint, taken as correct at the initial stage, did not establish that the appellant was acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty.

Since the complaint did not show the necessary nexus between the alleged criminal acts and the appellant's official functions, the court concluded that no prior sanction was required for the magistrate to take cognizance of the offence.
